title.rendered: Hot Water Tank Maintenance: A Complete Homeowner’s Guide

content.rendered:
Why Hot Water Tank Maintenance Is Worth Your Time

Your hot water tank works around the clock, yet most homeowners don’t think about it until they step into a cold shower or find water pooling on the basement floor. The good news is that regular hot water tank maintenance is simple, affordable, and one of the best ways to avoid an expensive emergency replacement.

This guide covers why maintenance matters, what you can do yourself, and when to call a professional for hot water tank service in Vancouver.

Why Hot Water Tank Maintenance Matters

A typical tank-style water heater lasts 8 to 12 years, but that lifespan depends heavily on how well it’s looked after. Consistent water heater maintenance offers several benefits:

  • Longer tank life: Removing sediment and replacing worn parts slows internal corrosion.
  • Lower energy bills: A clean, well-tuned tank heats water more efficiently.
  • Fewer breakdowns: Small problems get caught before they become failures.
  • Better safety: Pressure valves, gas connections, and venting are checked regularly.
  • More consistent hot water: Less sediment means more usable capacity in the tank.

Skipping maintenance doesn’t just shorten the life of your heater. It can lead to water damage, which often costs far more than the tank itself.

Signs Your Tank Needs Attention

Before we get into the routine, watch for these warning signs that your system needs a hot water tank inspection sooner rather than later:

  • Rumbling, popping, or banging noises from the tank
  • Rusty or discoloured hot water
  • Water that takes longer to heat or runs out quickly
  • Moisture or small leaks around the base
  • Fluctuating water temperature
  • A tank older than 10 years

If you notice any of these, don’t wait for the next scheduled check-up.

Hot Water Heater Maintenance Checklist

Here are the core tasks every homeowner should know about. Some are easy DIY jobs, while others are best left to a licensed technician.

Inspect the Tank and Surroundings

Once a month, do a quick visual check. Look for rust, moisture, corrosion around fittings, and leaks at the base or pipe connections. Make sure the area around the tank is clear of storage, since gas and electric units both need space and airflow. A small drip today can signal a failing tank tomorrow.

Test the Temperature and Pressure Relief Valve

The temperature and pressure (T&P) relief valve is a critical safety device that releases pressure if the tank overheats. Test it about once a year by lifting the lever briefly. Water should flow out and the valve should snap back and stop. If it leaks continuously, doesn’t release water, or looks corroded, it needs to be replaced by a professional. Never cap or block this valve.

Flush the Tank (Hot Water Tank Cleaning)

Over time, minerals settle at the bottom of the tank as sediment. This layer forces your heater to work harder, reduces efficiency, and can cause noise and premature failure. Hot water tank cleaning through an annual flush removes that buildup.

The basic process looks like this:

  • Turn off the power (electric) or set the gas control to “pilot” or off.
  • Shut off the cold water supply to the tank.
  • Attach a garden hose to the drain valve and run it to a floor drain or outside.
  • Open a hot water tap in the house, then open the drain valve.
  • Let the tank empty completely, then briefly open the cold supply to stir up and flush remaining sediment.
  • Close the drain valve, refill the tank fully, and only then restore power or gas.

Metro Vancouver’s municipal water is relatively soft, so sediment tends to build up more slowly than in hard-water regions. However, it still accumulates, particularly in older tanks, so annual flushing remains good practice. If your tank has never been flushed, or it’s several years old, have a professional handle it. Old drain valves can crack or clog, and a first-time flush on an aging tank can sometimes expose existing problems.

Check the Anode Rod

The anode rod is a “sacrificial” metal rod that attracts corrosive elements so they attack the rod instead of your tank lining. Once it’s consumed, the tank itself begins to corrode. Inspecting it every two to three years, and replacing it when it’s heavily worn, is one of the most effective ways to extend tank life. This is a task best done during professional hot water tank servicing, since the rod can be difficult to remove without the right tools.

Adjust the Temperature Setting

Most tanks should be set to around 60°C (140°F) at the tank. This is hot enough to inhibit bacterial growth such as Legionella, while mixing valves or tempering devices can bring the temperature at your taps down to a safer level, around 49°C (120°F), to reduce scald risk. Setting it higher wastes energy, and setting it much lower can create health concerns.

Inspect Venting, Burners, and Connections

For gas-fired tanks, the burner, pilot or ignition system, venting, and gas connections all need to be checked for safe, efficient operation. Soot, a yellow or flickering flame, or a smell of gas are all reasons to shut the unit off and call a professional immediately. This part of water heater maintenance should never be a DIY job.

What a Professional Hot Water Tank Tune-Up Includes

While homeowners can handle the basics, an annual hot water tank tune-up by a qualified technician gives you peace of mind and catches issues you may not see. A thorough tune-up typically includes:

  • Complete hot water tank inspection of the tank, fittings, and piping
  • Flushing and cleaning the tank to remove sediment
  • Testing the T&P relief valve and other safety controls
  • Inspecting the anode rod and replacing it if needed
  • Checking burners, ignition, venting, and gas connections (gas models)
  • Checking heating elements and thermostats (electric models)
  • Verifying temperature settings and overall performance
  • Advice on the remaining lifespan of your unit

A professional visit also creates a service record, which is useful for warranty purposes and when you sell your home.

How Often Should You Schedule Hot Water Tank Maintenance?

A good rule of thumb:

Task Frequency
Visual check for leaks and rust Monthly
T&P valve test Yearly
Tank flush Yearly
Professional tune-up and inspection Yearly
Anode rod inspection Every 2–3 years

If your tank is over eight years old, or your household uses a lot of hot water, consider more frequent check-ups.

Maintenance vs. Replacement: Knowing When to Let Go

Even with excellent care, every tank eventually reaches the end of its life. Consider replacement if your tank is over 10–12 years old and showing signs of rust, repeated leaks, or declining performance. A leaking tank cannot be repaired, because the failure is inside the tank itself. A newer, more efficient model, or a high-efficiency or tankless option, may also lower your utility bills, so a good technician can help you compare repair and replacement costs honestly.

Why Choose Local Hot Water Tank Maintenance in Vancouver?

Local expertise matters. A Vancouver-based technician understands regional building codes, typical home setups, and the water conditions in the Lower Mainland, and can respond quickly if something goes wrong. Whether you need routine hot water tank maintenance in Vancouver, an inspection before selling your home, or help with a tank that’s acting up, working with an experienced local team means faster service and advice tailored to your home.

Final Thoughts

Regular hot water tank maintenance is a small investment that pays off with longer equipment life, lower energy use, and fewer unpleasant surprises. Combine simple monthly checks and an annual flush with a professional tune-up, and your tank will be far more likely to deliver reliable hot water for years to come.

title.rendered: Why Fall Is the Best Time for Furnace Maintenance

content.rendered:
As temperatures begin to drop across Canada, preparing your home for winter becomes a priority. One of the most important steps is making sure your heating system is ready to keep your family comfortable throughout the colder months. Scheduling furnace maintenance in the fall helps identify potential issues early, improve heating efficiency, and reduce the risk of unexpected breakdowns when you need heat the most.

Regular maintenance can also help extend your furnace’s lifespan and support consistent indoor comfort. Whether you have a gas furnace or a boiler-based heating system, a professional inspection before winter can help you avoid unnecessary stress and costly repairs.

Prevent Unexpected Furnace Breakdowns

The last thing you want during a Canadian winter is a furnace that stops working on a freezing night. After months of limited use, your heating system may have developed issues such as dirty components, worn parts, or ignition problems.

Fall is an ideal time to arrange furnace maintenance because a qualified technician can inspect the system, identify potential concerns, and recommend repairs before temperatures fall further.

Addressing minor issues early can help reduce the likelihood of inconvenient breakdowns during the busiest part of the heating season.

Improve Heating Efficiency and Manage Energy Costs

A furnace that has not been maintained properly may need to work harder to heat your home. Dirty filters, restricted airflow, and neglected components can affect its performance and contribute to unnecessary energy use.

Professional heating system maintenance services help keep your equipment operating as intended. Depending on your system, maintenance may include inspecting key components, checking airflow, cleaning accessible parts, and verifying safe operation.

A well-maintained furnace can distribute heat more consistently and may help manage energy consumption throughout winter. However, actual savings depend on your furnace’s age, condition, efficiency, and how you use your heating system.

Improve Home Comfort Before Winter

Uneven temperatures, weak airflow, and rooms that take too long to warm up can indicate that your heating system needs attention.

Scheduling maintenance in the fall gives technicians time to check for common performance issues before your furnace is running regularly. They can assess the system’s operation and identify concerns that may affect heating consistency.

With your furnace inspected before winter arrives, you can feel more confident that your home will stay comfortable when outdoor temperatures drop.

Support a Longer Furnace Lifespan

A furnace is a significant investment, and homeowners naturally want to get the most value from it. Regular maintenance helps identify wear and tear before minor problems develop into more serious issues.

During a professional inspection, a technician can check important components, assess system performance, and identify parts that may need attention. Keeping up with recommended maintenance can help reduce avoidable strain on your equipment and support its long-term reliability.

Although maintenance cannot prevent every failure, it is an important part of caring for your heating system.

Improve Heating System Safety

Safety is another important reason to schedule furnace maintenance before winter. Gas furnaces and other combustion-based heating systems require proper inspection to help identify potential operating or ventilation problems.

A qualified technician can check relevant safety controls, inspect accessible components, and assess the system according to the manufacturer’s recommendations.

Homeowners should also make sure their carbon monoxide alarms are installed and working properly. Carbon monoxide is an odourless, colourless gas that can be dangerous. If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, leave the building immediately and contact emergency services from a safe location.

Never ignore unusual furnace smells, repeated shutdowns, or signs of improper operation. Arrange a professional inspection if you notice anything concerning.

Avoid the Winter Rush for Furnace Repairs

Heating contractors often receive more service requests when temperatures drop and furnaces begin running continuously. Waiting until your system stops working can mean dealing with an urgent repair when you need heat most.

Booking furnace maintenance in the fall gives you an opportunity to arrange a convenient appointment before peak winter demand. If the technician identifies a problem, there may also be more time to plan the necessary repair before colder weather arrives.

Preventive maintenance does not eliminate every repair, but it can help you prepare for the heating season with fewer surprises.

How Often to Do Furnace Maintenance

If you are wondering how often to do furnace maintenance, a professional inspection once a year is a good general guideline for most residential furnaces. Scheduling the appointment in early fall, before regular heating begins, is a practical way to prepare for winter.

Your maintenance schedule may vary depending on the equipment type, age, usage, and manufacturer’s recommendations.

Here are a few simple ways to care for your heating system between professional visits:

  • Check your air filter regularly: Inspect it according to the manufacturer’s instructions and replace it when needed.
  • Keep vents clear: Avoid blocking supply vents and return-air grilles with furniture, rugs, or other items.
  • Keep the area around the furnace clear: Follow the manufacturer’s clearance requirements and keep combustible materials away from the equipment.
  • Pay attention to warning signs: Unusual noises, inconsistent heating, frequent cycling, or unexplained increases in energy use may indicate a problem.
  • Follow recommended servicing intervals: Arrange professional inspections and maintenance as specified by the equipment manufacturer or your HVAC technician.

These simple steps support regular maintenance, but they do not replace a professional inspection.

What Does Professional Furnace Maintenance Include?

The exact maintenance process depends on your heating equipment, but a professional service visit may include:

  • Inspecting the heat exchanger and other relevant components, where accessible and appropriate.
  • Checking the burner, ignition system, and safety controls on applicable systems.
  • Inspecting electrical connections and testing system operation.
  • Checking airflow and inspecting the air filter.
  • Assessing the venting system and combustion-related components, where applicable.
  • Identifying signs of wear, damage, or performance issues.
  • Providing recommendations for any required furnace repair and maintenance.

Not every task applies to every furnace. Your technician should follow the manufacturer’s service requirements and the needs of your specific system.

Don’t Forget Furnace Boiler Maintenance

Homes with boiler-based heating systems also benefit from seasonal servicing. While a furnace typically heats and circulates air, a boiler heats water or another fluid to provide warmth through radiators, baseboards, or hydronic radiant heating.

Furnace boiler maintenance should be tailored to the equipment installed in your home. For a boiler, a technician may inspect operating controls, check for leaks, assess pressure and temperature settings, and examine relevant venting and safety components.

Because furnaces and boilers operate differently, they require different maintenance procedures. Make sure you arrange service for the specific heating system you use rather than assuming that the same checklist applies to both.

When Should You Call for Furnace Repair and Maintenance?

Routine maintenance is intended to keep your system in good working condition, while repairs address faults that have already developed. Sometimes, an inspection reveals an issue that requires more than standard servicing.

Contact an HVAC professional if you notice:

  • Your furnace is not producing enough heat.
  • The system turns on and off more frequently than usual.
  • You hear unusual banging, rattling, or grinding sounds.
  • Heating bills rise unexpectedly without an obvious explanation.
  • The furnace repeatedly shuts down or struggles to start.
  • You notice unusual odours or signs of improper operation.

If you smell gas, leave the building without operating electrical switches or using open flames, and contact your gas utility or emergency services from a safe location. Do not attempt to troubleshoot a suspected gas leak yourself.

Prompt professional attention can help determine whether your system needs a repair, a maintenance adjustment, or further investigation.

Get Your Heating System Ready for Winter with Airlinx Heating

Fall is the ideal time to prepare your heating system for the colder months ahead. From improving operating efficiency to identifying potential problems before they become urgent, regular furnace maintenance helps you approach winter with greater confidence.

Whether you need a routine inspection, help with an existing heating issue, or servicing a boiler-based system, professional attention can help keep your equipment operating safely and reliably.

Contact Airlinx Heating to discuss your heating system maintenance needs and arrange service before winter arrives. A little preparation now can make a big difference to your home’s comfort throughout the heating season.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is fall the best time for furnace maintenance?

Yes. Early fall is a practical time to schedule furnace maintenance because it allows you to inspect and service your system before it is needed regularly during winter. It also gives you time to address any issues before colder weather arrives.

How often should a furnace be serviced?

Most residential furnaces should receive professional maintenance approximately once a year, subject to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Fall is generally a convenient time to schedule this service.

Can furnace maintenance help lower energy bills?

It can help your system operate as intended by addressing issues such as restricted airflow and neglected components. However, the amount you save depends on the furnace’s condition, age, efficiency, and usage.

Is furnace maintenance necessary if my heating system seems to be working properly?

Yes. Some developing problems may not be obvious during normal operation. Regular maintenance helps identify potential concerns early and supports reliable heating throughout winter.

What is the difference between furnace maintenance and furnace repair?

Furnace maintenance involves routine inspection, cleaning, testing, and preventive care. Furnace repair focuses on diagnosing and fixing an existing fault, such as an ignition issue or a malfunctioning component.

Do boilers also need annual maintenance?

Most residential boilers benefit from regular professional servicing, often annually, depending on the manufacturer’s guidance and system requirements. A technician can recommend the appropriate maintenance schedule for your specific boiler.

title.rendered: How Does A Tankless Hot Water Heater Work? A Guide for Canadian Homeowners

content.rendered:
If you have ever stepped into a cold shower because someone else used up the hot water, you have probably thought about upgrading. So, how does a tankless hot water heater work, and is it right for your home or business?

In this guide, Airlinx Heating explains how a tankless water heater operates, what it costs, how to maintain it, and when a commercial unit makes sense.

What Is A Tankless Water Heater?

A tankless water heater, also called an on-demand water heater, heats water only when you need it. A traditional storage tank keeps 150 to 270 litres of water hot around the clock, even when nobody is home. A tankless unit has no storage tank and delivers hot water directly to your tap, shower, or appliance.

Because it isn’t constantly reheating stored water, a tankless system wastes less energy. It also takes up much less space, since most units are compact and wall-mounted.

How Does A Tankless Hot Water Heater Work? Step by Step

It’s easy, and it happens in seconds : 

  1. You switch on the hot water tap.  Cold water flows in through the pipe to the water heater. 
  2. A flow sensor indicates movement of water. This prompts the heater to turn on.
  3. The heating component is activated. In the case of a gas-based heating system, a burner is ignited. In the case of an electric heating system, heating elements will undergo the process.
  4. The water goes through a heat exchanger. The water is heated as it moves through until it reaches the desired temperature of 49°C (120°F).
  5. Hot water flows to your fixture. You get a steady supply for as long as the tap is open.
  6. You turn off the tap. The sensor detects that the flow has stopped, and the unit shuts down. No energy is used until you need hot water again.

Gas vs. Electric Tankless Water Heaters

  • Gas (natural gas or propane): These typically deliver a higher flow rate, so they suit larger homes with several bathrooms. They need proper venting.
  • Electric: These are compact and easier to install, and often suit smaller homes, condos, or point-of-use applications. They draw significant electrical power, so your panel capacity matters.

Understanding Flow Rate and Temperature Rise

Tankless heaters are sized by flow rate (litres per minute) and temperature rise (the difference between incoming cold water and your target temperature). 

This matters in Canada, where winter groundwater can be very cold, so a unit that performs well in summer may struggle in January if it is undersized. A professional assessment helps you choose the right capacity.

Benefits of A Tankless Water Heater

  • Endless hot water: No more running out mid-shower.
  • Energy efficiency: You heat water only when needed, which can lower utility bills.
  • Space savings: The wall-mounted design frees up floor space.
  • Longer lifespan: Tankless units often last 20 years or more with proper care, compared with roughly 10 to 15 years for many tanks.
  • Reduced risk of tank leaks: There is no large tank to rupture and flood your basement.

Cost Of Tankless Water Heater And Installation

The cost of a tankless water heater and installation varies with the type, capacity, and complexity of the job. As a general guide, many Canadian homeowners can expect:

  • Unit cost: Roughly $1,000 to $3,000+, depending on brand, fuel type, and capacity
  • Installation: Often $1,000 to $3,000+, depending on venting, gas line sizing, electrical upgrades, and removal of the old tank
  • Total typical range: About $2,500 to $6,000, with larger or more complex setups costing more

These are general estimates only. For an accurate price, request a quote based on your home’s needs.

What affects the price?

  • Gas vs. electric
  • Whether you’re replacing a tank or installing in a new location
  • Venting requirements (direct vent, power vent)
  • Upgrades to the gas line or electrical panel
  • Number of fixtures and household hot water demand

Tankless units cost more upfront than tank heaters, but energy savings and a longer lifespan often make up the difference over time. It’s also worth checking for federal, provincial, or utility rebates on high-efficiency models.

Tankless Hot Water Heater Maintenance

Good tankless hot water heater maintenance protects your investment and keeps performance consistent. Key tasks include:

  • Annual descaling (flushing): Mineral buildup, especially in hard-water areas, can reduce efficiency and damage the heat exchanger. Flushing with a descaling solution removes it.
  • Clean or replace the inlet water filter: A clogged screen restricts flow.
  • Inspect the venting: Check for blockages, corrosion, or leaks in gas models.
  • Check for error codes: Most units display codes that point to problems early.
  • Schedule a professional tune-up: A licensed technician can inspect the burner, sensors, and heat exchanger to keep everything running safely.

If you have hard water, consider a water softener to extend the life of the unit.

Commercial Tankless Water Heater: Is It Right for Your Business?

A commercial tankless water heater works on the same principle as a residential unit but is built for higher demand. Restaurants, hotels, gyms, salons, offices, and multi-unit buildings often use them because they:

  • Deliver continuous hot water during peak periods
  • Can be linked together (cascaded) to scale up capacity
  • Save valuable floor space compared with large storage tanks
  • Reduce standby energy loss in buildings with fluctuating demand

Sizing a commercial system takes careful calculation of peak demand, so it’s best handled by experienced heating professionals.

Is A Tankless Water Heater Worth It?

For many households and businesses, yes. If you want an endless hot water supply, lower standby energy waste, a smaller footprint, and a longer-lasting system, a tankless unit is a strong option. It may be less ideal if upfront cost is your main concern or if your home needs significant gas line or electrical upgrades.

Final Thoughts: How Does A Tankless Hot Water Heater Work for You?

So, how does a tankless hot water heater work? It senses demand, heats water instantly as it passes through a heat exchanger, and shuts off when you’re done. The result is a steady supply of hot water without the energy waste of a storage tank.

Whether you’re considering a residential upgrade or a commercial tankless water heater for your business, choosing the right size, type, and installer makes all the difference.

content.rendered:
Boiler maintenance is the most effective way to keep your heating reliable, safe, and affordable through a Vancouver winter. With the cold, wet season here, now is the time to find out whether your boiler is ready, not the night it stops working.

Whether you own a home in Burnaby, manage a building in Richmond or run a commercial property in Vancouver, a boiler that is serviced regularly uses less fuel, breaks down less often and lasts longer. In this guide, the team at Airlinx Heating explains what a boiler maintenance service includes, how often you need one, what you can check yourself, and when to call a professional.

What Is Boiler Maintenance and Why Does It Matter?

Boiler maintenance is a scheduled inspection, cleaning, and test of your boiler and its safety controls, so small faults are fixed before they become failures. It applies to every type of system, from a hot water boiler feeding radiators and in-floor heat to a steam boiler in a larger building.

Here is what regular maintenance protects:

  • Safety: A boiler burns fuel and vents combustion gases. Worn seals, a blocked flue, or a faulty control can allow dangerous leaks, including carbon monoxide.
  • Efficiency: Dirty burners and scaled heat exchangers make the boiler work harder and burn more fuel for the same heat.
  • Reliability: Many winter breakdowns start as worn parts that a technician would have spotted during a routine visit.
  • Lifespan: A boiler that is cleaned, tested, and adjusted each year typically lasts longer than one that is ignored.
  • Warranty: Many manufacturers expect proof of regular servicing before they honour a warranty claim.

Boiler Maintenance Service: What to Expect From a Professional Visit

A professional boiler maintenance service is a hands-on visit by a qualified technician who inspects, cleans, tests, and adjusts your system. For a typical home boiler, the visit often takes one to two hours, depending on the size and condition of the unit.

  1. Conversation: You describe anything unusual: noises, pressure drops, cold radiators, slow hot water, or a rising fuel bill.
  2. Visual inspection: The technician checks the boiler, piping, valves, venting, and the room around it for leaks, corrosion, soot, or scorch marks.
  3. Cleaning and testing: Burners, heat exchanger surfaces, and key components are cleaned, then safety controls are tested to confirm they shut the boiler down when they should.
  4. Combustion check: Using a gas analyzer, the technician measures how cleanly the boiler burns and adjusts it for safe, efficient operation.
  5. Report and advice: You receive a clear explanation of what was found, what needs attention now and what can wait, with an estimate before any extra work begins.

In British Columbia, gas appliance work must be done by a licensed gas contractor with certified gas fitters, so always confirm credentials before you book.

Boiler Servicing and Maintenance Checklist

Good boiler servicing and maintenance follows a repeatable checklist. Use this table to see what a thorough visit covers, or to compare quotes from different contractors.

Component What the technician does Why it matters
Burner and ignition Cleans, inspects, and checks the flame pattern A clean, steady flame burns fuel safely and efficiently
Heat exchanger Inspects for soot, scale, corrosion and cracks Buildup wastes fuel; cracks are a safety risk
Venting and flue Checks for blockages, leaks and corrosion Keeps combustion gases out of the building
Safety controls Tests limit controls, low-water cut-off and pressure relief valve These are your last line of defence
Water pressure and expansion tank Checks pressure and tank condition Prevents pressure faults and valve discharge
Circulator pumps and zone valves Confirms they run quietly and respond to the thermostat Delivers even heat to every room
Condensate drain (condensing boilers) Clears and tests the trap and drain line Blockages can shut the boiler down
Thermostat and controls Tests settings and operation Improves comfort and cuts wasted fuel
Combustion and carbon monoxide Measures exhaust gases with an analyzer Confirms the boiler is burning safely

Annual Boiler Maintenance: How Often and When to Book

Annual boiler maintenance, one full service every 12 months, is the standard recommendation for nearly every boiler. Older units, heavily used systems, and boilers in rental or commercial buildings may benefit from extra checks during the heating season.

The best time to book is early autumn, before the first cold snap, when technicians have the most availability. If you have not had your boiler serviced yet this year, do it now rather than waiting for the first freeze, when emergency calls are at their highest.

A yearly service pays you back in several ways:

  • Lower fuel use, because a clean, correctly adjusted boiler wastes less energy.
  • Fewer surprise breakdowns during the coldest weeks.
  • Early warning of parts that are wearing out, so you can budget for repairs instead of reacting to them.
  • A documented service history, which supports warranty claims and adds confidence when you sell the property.

Home Boiler Maintenance: What You Can Do Yourself

Home boiler maintenance starts with simple checks between professional visits. These take a few minutes and help you catch problems early:

  • Check the pressure gauge. Many home boilers sit around 12 to 15 psi when cold, but follow the range in your owner’s manual. Repeated drops can point to a leak.
  • Look and listen. Banging, whistling, or gurgling, damp patches, or rust around the boiler are all reasons to call for service.
  • Watch the flame. On a boiler with a viewing window, a steady blue flame is normal. Yellow or flickering flames need a technician.
  • Keep the area clear. Leave space around the boiler and never store paint, cleaners, or other flammables nearby.
  • Clear outdoor vents. Make sure exhaust and air intake pipes are free of leaves, snow, and debris.
  • Bleed radiators. If radiators are cold at the top, trapped air is a likely cause.
  • Test your carbon monoxide and smoke alarms. Replace batteries on schedule.

Leave the rest to a licensed professional. Opening the burner compartment, adjusting gas pressure, replacing safety controls, and repairing leaks are not do-it-yourself jobs. They involve gas, high temperatures, and pressurized water, and a mistake can be dangerous.

Commercial Boiler Maintenance: Protecting Uptime and Compliance

Commercial boiler maintenance has higher stakes than home service. When a boiler fails in an office, apartment building, school, restaurant, or warehouse, the cost is not just a repair bill. It has lost comfort for tenants, disrupted operations, and, in some buildings, unsafe conditions.

A good commercial maintenance program usually includes:

  • Planned, scheduled visits timed around your building’s operating hours, so work does not disrupt occupants.
  • Larger-system checks, including multiple boilers, headers, pumps, water treatment, and building control integration.
  • Water quality and blowdown checks, which protect heat exchangers from scale and corrosion.
  • Combustion tuning to keep large burners efficient, since small efficiency losses add up quickly at scale.
  • Written service records for insurers, property managers and inspectors.

Regulations also matter. In BC, Technical Safety BC oversees boilers and pressure equipment, and requirements for permits and inspections depend on the type and size of the equipment. Ask your contractor to confirm what applies to your building.

Airlinx Heating supports commercial properties across Vancouver and nearby areas. Learn more about our commercial HVAC services.

Boiler Repair Maintenance Services: Warning Signs You Should Not Ignore

Even a well-maintained boiler can develop faults. Catching them early is what boiler repair maintenance services are for, because a minor repair now is far cheaper than a failed boiler in January. Call a technician if you notice any of these:

  • No heat or no hot water, or heat that is uneven between rooms
  • Banging, kettling (a rumbling like a boiling kettle), whistling, or gurgling noises
  • Water around the boiler or dripping from pipes and valves
  • Pressure that keeps dropping or rises too high
  • A yellow or orange flame, or soot around the burner
  • The boiler shutting off repeatedly or the pilot light going out
  • A noticeable rise in heating costs with no change in use

Safety first: if you smell gas or a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, leave the building immediately and call 911 and your gas utility’s emergency line from outside. Do not try to restart the boiler.

title.rendered: Heat Pump Vs Air Conditioning Unit: Which is Best in Burnaby?

content.rendered:
If you’ve been sweating through Burnaby’s increasingly warm summers while also dreading the damp chill of our coastal winters, you’ve probably found yourself comparing a heat pump vs air conditioning unit and wondering which one actually makes sense for your home. It’s one of the most common questions homeowners in the Lower Mainland ask us, and honestly, there isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. It depends on your home, your budget, and how you actually use your space throughout the year.

Let’s break it down so you can make a decision that fits your household, not just a sales pitch.

What is a Heat Pump and How Does it Work

Before comparing the two, it helps to understand what a heat pump is and how it works. Unlike a furnace that burns fuel to create heat, a heat pump moves heat from one place to another. In the winter, it extracts warmth from the outside air (yes, even cold air holds thermal energy) and pumps it inside your home. In the summer, it simply reverses the cycle, pulling heat out of your house and releasing it outdoors functioning exactly like an air conditioner.

This dual functionality is the biggest draw of heat pump air conditioning systems. You get heating and cooling from a single unit, which is a huge advantage in a climate like Burnaby’s, where winters are mild enough that a heat pump can handle most of your heating needs without backup, while summers are warm enough to justify proper cooling.

Air Conditioning Units: The Traditional Cooling Choice

A standalone air conditioning unit, on the other hand, does one job: it cools. It works by cycling refrigerant through indoor and outdoor coils, absorbing heat from inside your home and releasing it outside. It’s a tried-and-tested technology, and for homes that already have a reliable furnace for winter heating, adding a dedicated AC unit for summer comfort can be a straightforward, cost-effective solution.

The catch is that you’re running two separate systems: a furnace for winter and an AC unit for summer which means two systems to maintain, repair, and eventually replace.

Comparing Costs: Heat Pump vs Air Conditioning Unit

Cost is usually the deciding factor for most Burnaby homeowners, so let’s talk numbers.

The cost of air conditioning installation on its own tends to be lower upfront than installing a full heat pump system, simply because you’re only paying for a cooling appliance. If your furnace is still in good shape and you just want relief from summer heat, a standalone AC unit might seem like the cheaper route initially.

However, when you factor in the cost of fitting air conditioning alongside the ongoing expense of running a separate gas or electric furnace, the math starts to shift. Heat pumps are more energy-efficient than furnaces for most of the year in our mild coastal climate, which often means lower utility bills over time. Many Burnaby homeowners also qualify for rebates through BC Hydro and FortisBC when switching to a heat pump, which can significantly offset the initial investment.

So while a heat pump typically has a higher upfront air conditioning unit installation cost compared to a basic AC system, it can pay for itself over a few years through energy savings and rebate programs plus you’re getting heating and cooling in one package instead of two separate systems.

Which One Suits Burnaby’s Climate Better?

Burnaby sits in a temperate coastal zone. Our winters rarely dip to extreme lows for extended periods, and our summers, while getting hotter each year with more frequent heat waves, aren’t as brutal as inland or prairie climates. This kind of moderate climate is actually ideal for heat pumps.

Because heat pumps don’t have to fight against extreme cold, they can operate efficiently through most of a Burnaby winter, only needing backup heating during the rare deep freeze. And when summer rolls around, that same unit switches over and cools your home just as effectively as a standard air conditioner.

If you live in an older Burnaby home with an aging furnace, replacing it with a heat pump system often makes more financial and practical sense than installing a separate AC unit and keeping an outdated furnace running for another decade.

Don’t Forget Maintenance

Whichever system you choose, regular upkeep matters. Air conditioning maintenance things like cleaning coils, replacing filters, checking refrigerant levels, and inspecting ductwork keeps your system running efficiently and extends its lifespan. The same applies to heat pumps, which technically need a bit more attention since they run year-round rather than just in summer.

Skipping maintenance is one of the fastest ways to see your energy bills creep up and your system fail earlier than it should. A quick seasonal check-up from a licensed technician can catch small issues before they become expensive repairs.

So, Which Should You Choose?

Here’s the honest, no-fluff answer:

  • Choose a heat pump if your furnace is aging, you want to reduce your carbon footprint, you’re eligible for rebates, or you want one system that handles both heating and cooling efficiently in Burnaby’s mild climate.
  • Choose a standalone air conditioning unit if your furnace is relatively new and reliable, your budget is tighter right now, and you mainly need summer cooling without touching your heating setup.

Both options work well in Burnaby; it really comes down to your home’s current setup, how long you plan to stay in it, and how much you value long-term efficiency versus lower upfront costs.

Get Expert Advice for Your Burnaby Home

Every home is different, and the best way to decide between a heat pump and an air conditioning unit is to have a professional assess your space, your existing HVAC setup, and your budget. Our team at Airlinx Heating has helped countless Burnaby homeowners navigate this exact decision, and we’re happy to walk you through your options, provide accurate cost estimates, and recommend the system that actually fits your home rather than pushing a one-size-fits-all solution.

Reach out today for a free consultation, and let’s figure out the best heating and cooling solution for your Burnaby home.

content.rendered:
If you’ve ever wondered what is HVAC while reading a home listing, getting a repair quote, or noticing your energy bill creep up, you’re not alone. HVAC is one of those terms everyone hears but few people fully understand  until something breaks down on the coldest night of the year. This guide breaks down what does HVAC stand for, how the system works, and why choosing the right HVAC contractor matters just as much as the equipment itself.

Whether you’re a homeowner in Burnaby researching HVAC Services Burnaby or a business owner planning an upgrade, this guide will give you a clear, practical understanding of your heating and cooling system.

What Does HVAC Stand For?

Let’s start with the basics. HVAC meaning: HVAC stands for Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning. It’s the umbrella term for the systems and equipment responsible for regulating indoor temperature, humidity, and air quality in homes, offices, and commercial buildings.

So, what is Heating Ventilation and Air Conditioning, exactly? It’s the combination of three connected functions:

  • Heating – Warms indoor spaces during cold months using furnaces, boilers, or heat pumps.
  • Ventilation – Circulates and exchanges air to remove pollutants, odors, and excess moisture while bringing in fresh outdoor air.
  • Air Conditioning – Cools and dehumidifies indoor air during warmer months for comfort and air quality control.

Together, these three components work as a single integrated system to keep your indoor environment comfortable, healthy, and energy-efficient year-round.

How Does an HVAC System Work?

An HVAC system doesn’t just “make it warm” or “make it cool”  it’s a coordinated network of components working together:

  1. Thermostat – Sets the desired temperature and signals the system to turn on or off.
  2. Furnace or Heat Pump – Generates or transfers heat throughout the building.
  3. Air Conditioner or Heat Pump (Cooling Mode) – Removes heat and humidity from indoor air.
  4. Ductwork – Distributes conditioned air throughout the space.
  5. Ventilation System – Exchanges stale indoor air for fresh outdoor air.
  6. Air Filters – Trap dust, allergens, and particles to improve indoor air quality.

When one part of this chain isn’t working properly, comfort and efficiency suffer  which is why professional HVAC installation and regular upkeep are so important.

Why HVAC Systems Matter for Your Home or Business

A well-functioning HVAC system does more than control temperature. It affects:

  • Indoor air quality – Filtering allergens, dust, and pollutants
  • Energy efficiency – Reducing utility costs through optimized performance
  • Comfort – Maintaining consistent temperature and humidity year-round
  • Property value – Modern, efficient systems are a selling point for homes and commercial buildings
  • Health and safety – Preventing mold growth, poor air circulation, and carbon monoxide risks

This is why investing in the right HVAC solutions, not just any equipment, but a system matched to your building’s size and needs  makes a measurable difference over time.

Types of HVAC Services You Should Know About

Understanding HVAC services helps you know what to expect and when to call a professional.

1. HVAC Installation

New construction, renovations, or replacing an outdated system all require professional HVAC installation. Correct sizing and setup at this stage prevent years of inefficiency and costly repairs down the road.

2. HVAC Maintenance Service

Routine HVAC maintenance service including filter changes, coil cleaning, and system inspections  extends equipment lifespan, keeps warranties valid, and catches small issues before they become expensive breakdowns.

3. Repairs and Troubleshooting

From strange noises to inconsistent temperatures, a qualified technician can diagnose and fix issues before they escalate.

4. Emergency Heating and Cooling Service

Furnace failures in winter or air conditioning breakdowns in summer rarely happen at a convenient time. A reliable emergency heating and cooling service ensures you’re never left without comfort or safety when it matters most.

Choosing the Right HVAC Contractor

Not all technicians are created equal. When selecting an HVAC contractor or air conditioning contractor, look for:

  • Licensed, insured, and certified technicians
  • Transparent, upfront pricing
  • Experience with both residential and commercial systems
  • Positive local reviews and references
  • Availability for emergency calls
  • Manufacturer-backed warranties on parts and labor

A trustworthy contractor doesn’t just fix the immediate problem, they help you understand your system and plan for long-term efficiency.

HVAC Services in Burnaby

If you’re searching for dependable HVAC Services Burnaby, local expertise matters. Weather patterns, building codes, and regional energy costs all influence what type of heating and cooling setup works best in this area. A local team understands these factors and can recommend solutions tailored to Burnaby homes and businesses, not generic, one-size-fits-all fixes.

At Airlinx Heating, our technicians specialize in everything from routine maintenance to full system installations, backed by local knowledge and responsive service.

Signs You Need Professional HVAC Help

Watch for these warning signs that it’s time to call a professional:

  • Uneven heating or cooling between rooms
  • Rising energy bills without increased usage
  • Strange noises, odors, or excessive dust
  • Frequent cycling on and off
  • Weak airflow from vents
  • System age of 10–15+ years

Catching these signs early  and scheduling regular HVAC maintenance service  can save you from a full system failure and costly emergency repairs.

Final Thoughts

So, what is HVAC? It’s the essential system that keeps your indoor environment safe, comfortable, and efficient  covering heating, ventilation, and air conditioning as one integrated network. Understanding how it works empowers you to make smarter decisions about installation, maintenance, and repairs.

Whether you need routine upkeep, a new system installation, or an emergency heating and cooling service, working with an experienced, licensed HVAC contractor ensures your investment pays off in comfort and reliability for years to come.

title.rendered: How to Keep Mice Out of Heat Pump and Prevent Costly Damage

content.rendered:
Have you ever opened up your outdoor unit only to see some chewed wires, shredded insulation, and even a suspicious nest hidden between panels? Well, then you know first-hand just how frustrating the presence of mice in your heat pump can get. Rodents are naturally attracted by warmth, safety, and quiet environment offered by your heat pump, particularly once the weather starts getting colder. A neglected rodent infestation can easily escalate from a tune-up to a pricey heat pump repair job.

But what you should know is that preventing mice from nesting in your heat pump doesn’t take too much effort. Some regular maintenance and prevention tips can save your heat pump from unnecessary problems. Read on to find out more.

Why Do Mice Like Heat Pumps?

Heat pumps are the perfect home for mice because of how warm and comfortable they are and how many places there are to hide. Throw in some leaves or tall grass in the surrounding area, and the mouse will feel right at home.

Mice are specifically drawn to:

  • The heat emitted from the refrigerant lines and electrical components
  • Hard-to-reach spots within the outer housing
  • Materials used for nesting such as leaves, grass, and loose insulation
  • Any nearby food or water sources, even if they are just a couple of feet away

As soon as the mice start to take up residence, you know that they will not be sitting idly by. They can chew the wires, nest the motor fans, or plug up condensate lines and drains. Each of these can result in short circuits, reduced air flow, or shut down your entire system.

Signs That You May Have a Mouse Problem

Before going into how to prevent mouse problems, it is important to recognize the signs. These include:

  • Droppings or pieces of nesting material inside or around the unit
  • Damaged wires or frayed insulation
  • Scurrying, scratching, or rustling noises from within the cabinet
  • A system that doesn’t work properly or turns off without reason
  • A damp or mildew smell, or even the smell of burning around the electrical panel
  • Weaker heating

It might be time to get a professional in there if you see any of these signs.

Easy Tips for Stopping Mice From Getting into Your Heat Pump

Clear the Area Around the Unit

Rodents love messiness, so the simplest first step would be to tidy up. Leave several feet of unobstructed area around the heat pump. It should not be surrounded by any leaves, mulch, and any other lawn debris. Also, cut off any bushes and branches touching the cabinet of the heat pump. Do not pile firewood and storage boxes nearby. If water is prone to accumulate in the soil close to the heat pump, solve this problem too. Wet soil, like hot one, will attract more pests.

A pleasant additional trick: some plants, such as rosemary, mint, lavender, and garlic are proven to repel mice. So plant them some distance away from the heat pump (not right next to it).

Seal the Openings

This is probably the best measure you can take. Rodents can squeeze into openings smaller than a coin. You should look for openings around:

  • Refrigerant line penetrations where pipes go through the wall or the heat pump itself
  • Wiring holes and conduit openings
  • Bottom panels, base pads, and access covers
  • Fan grills and cabinet seams

The fact that the cracks are filled by steel wool is a great way of sealing the space because the mice won’t chew through this material. The other two good options include stainless steel mesh or hardware cloth with openings of 1/4 inch, whereas the best way of achieving a permanent solution will be combining the steel wool with the silicone caulk. However, it is better not to use expanding foam because the mice will chew through it.

Add Physical Barriers

Beyond sealing, a few physical upgrades go a long way:

  • Fine wire mesh over vents and openings, while still allowing proper airflow
  • Line-set covers with tight-fitting ends
  • Elevating the unit slightly, since narrow legs or stands are harder for mice to climb
  • A small protective enclosure with fine mesh, as long as it doesn’t block ventilation

A qualified technician can install these without affecting how your heat pump system performs.

Go for Natural Deterrents

In case you want to go chemical-free, here are some natural deterrence methods that you may try:

  • Cotton balls dipped in peppermint oil at the entry points
  • Cedar shavings or pine shavings at the base
  • Dryer sheets or strongly scented bars of soap to be changed once in a while

You can also use ultrasonic deterrents as an additional option. Just remember not to put any poison close to the system. A mouse that dies inside the cabinet can create an even bigger mess and odor problem than the original infestation.

Why Maintenance Is Needed

It is necessary to maintain the heat pump system on a regular basis because it will help us to identify the cause of the problem in the early stages. In addition to maintaining the system, the technician will be able to detect any signs of nesting, clear the debris from the system, inspect the wiring, and check if there is any damage to the seals or access panels. It would be twice a year for most homeowners.

A Quick Prevention Checklist

  • Clear leaves, mulch, and vegetation from around the unit
  • Seal gaps with steel wool, mesh, or silicone
  • Install rodent guards or fine mesh screens
  • Use natural repellents near entry points
  • Book professional maintenance twice a year
  • Keep trash, pet food, and bird feeders away from the unit

When to Hire a Professional

As soon as you detect signs of nesting, damaged wiring, or any other changes which are affecting the performance of the heat pump system, you should turn to professionals for help and not try to fix the issue yourself. Doing the work related to electrical parts can be dangerous without proper knowledge and training, so a Airlinx will be able to do all the work right the first time in Burnaby and nearby areas.

Conclusion

Though mice are relatively small animals, their impact on a heat pump system is quite damaging and can cost a lot of money. But the good news is that all you need to prevent them from entering the system is just some preventive measures.

What is HVAC and how does it work?

Ventilation, heating, and air conditioning (HVAC) is a system that is used to regulate the humidity and temperature of your indoor spaces. It is an innovative technology that has changed over the years. With Airlinx heating and air-conditioning services, you get the best HVAC services.

The three main components of an HVAC system are the evaporator, condenser, and compressor. The work of a compressor is to pump coolant through the system. Then comes the evaporator, which removes heat from the air.

HVAC systems are used in both commercial and residential locations. These can be either decentralized or centralized. Centralized systems are more common in huge buildings, whereas decentralized units are common in smaller homes.

Most common types of HVAC systems:

Standard split systems:

A standard split system has an outdoor unit that envelopes the condenser and the compressor. This type of system is a good option for smaller homes because it is less expensive. Also, they are easier to maintain since the condenser and compressor units are present outside.

Do you know Packaged units?

A packaged unit is a self-contained HVAC system that has all the components in a single unit. The compressor, condenser, and evaporator are all clubbed together in the same outdoor unit. This is a good choice for larger homes because it is more efficient. Also, packaged units are much easier to install since everything is in the same place.

Heard about ductless mini-split systems?

It is similar to a standard split system, which does not use ductwork. It has one or more indoor units which are connected to an outdoor unit with the help of refrigerant lines. This is a good choice for homes or businesses that do not have existing ductwork.

Geothermal heat pumps are great:

A geothermal heat pump uses water to heat and cool your home. The water has a constant temperature that is lower than the air during hot days and cold in the winter.

This type of system is a good option for businesses and homes that can be very efficient. Also, geothermal heat pumps last more.

So, once you have your HVAC systems installed, it is necessary to keep up with regular maintenance. It helps in ensuring that your system is running efficiently and can prevent costly repairs. So, here are a few maintenance tips that will benefit you:

This is one of the most easiest and important things you can do to maintain your HVAC systems. Your filters need to be changed regularly every month or two. But this depends on the type of filter you have and the environment in which you live.

Cleaning your coils:

The condenser coils and the evaporator might get dirty over time. So, this reduces the efficiency of the system and causes it to work harder than it needs. Cleaning your coils at least once a year is the need of an hour.

Checking your ductwork:

Ductwork might leak over time. This results in higher energy bills and reduced indoor air quality. So, it is a good idea to get your ductwork checked every few years to make sure it is working properly.

HVAC repair tips:

 It might happen that even with regular maintenance, your HVAC systems can break down from time to time. So, here are a few tips for troubleshooting common HVAC problems:

Checking the thermostat:

If your system isn’t working, make sure you check the thermostat. There is a possibility that it might not be set correctly. So, get this fixed.

Checking the pilot light:

Your unit’s pilot is a crucial component. So, if it is out, the unit won’t function properly. Simply relight the pilot light and check to see if the unit starts functioning again.

If your system stops working suddenly, then the circuit breaker may have been tripped. This is common in houses that have older electrical systems.

title.rendered: How Does a Furnace Work? A Simple Guide to Home Heating

content.rendered:
Why It Helps to Know How Your Furnace Works

When the temperature drops, your furnace is the one appliance you expect to simply work. But if you have ever wondered how a furnace works, you are not alone. Knowing the basics helps you spot problems early, talk confidently with a technician, and keep your home warm without surprise repair bills.

This guide explains how a furnace heating system works in plain language. You will learn about the main furnace components, the gas furnace heating process, and the furnace heating cycle, from the moment your thermostat asks for heat to the moment warm air reaches your rooms.

What Is a Furnace Heating System?

A furnace heating system is a central heating appliance that warms air and distributes it through your home. Most Canadian homes use a forced-air design, which means a fan moves the heated air through a network of ducts and out of the vents in each room.

The idea is simple. The furnace creates heat from a fuel source, transfers that heat to the air, and sends the warm air where you need it. Natural gas is the most common fuel, though furnaces can also run on propane, oil, or electricity. Cooler air from the house returns to the furnace through return ducts, gets heated again, and the loop repeats until your home reaches the temperature you set.

Key Furnace Components and What They Do

To understand how a furnace works, it helps to meet the parts that make it happen. Here are the main furnace components and the role each one plays.

Furnace Thermostat

The thermostat is the brain of the operation. It measures the air temperature in your home and compares it with the setting you chose. When the room is too cool, it sends a signal to the furnace to start a heating cycle. When the room reaches the target temperature, it tells the furnace to shut off. Programmable and smart thermostats add scheduling, so the furnace heats only when it is needed.

Furnace Air Filter

The furnace air filter sits where air enters the furnace, usually in the return duct or a slot beside the blower. It catches dust, pet hair and other particles before they reach the blower and heat exchanger. A clean filter keeps air flowing freely and protects your equipment. A clogged filter restricts airflow, forces the furnace to work harder, and can cause overheating.

Furnace Blower

The furnace blower is a motor-driven fan that pulls cool air in from the return ducts, pushes it across the heat exchanger, and sends the warmed air through the supply ducts. It is the part that moves heat from the furnace to your living spaces. The blower can also run on its own to circulate air when the furnace is not heating.

Furnace Heat Exchanger

The heat exchanger is a set of metal chambers where the real heat transfer happens. Hot combustion gases from the burners flow through the inside of the heat exchanger and heat the metal. The blower pushes your household air across the outside surface, so the air picks up warmth without mixing with the combustion gases. Keeping those gases separate is essential for safety, which is why a cracked heat exchanger is a serious problem that needs a professional right away.

Other Parts Worth Knowing

  • Burners and gas valve: The gas valve releases natural gas to the burners, where it ignites and creates the flame.
  • Igniter: A hot surface igniter or electronic ignition lights the gas safely, replacing the old standing pilot light on most modern furnaces.
  • Flame sensor: This safety device confirms the burner is lit. If there is no flame, it shuts the gas off.
  • Inducer motor and flue: The inducer fan draws combustion gases through the system and out of the home through the vent pipe.
  • Control board: The circuit board manages the timing and safety checks for every step of the cycle.

The Gas Furnace Heating Process, Step by Step

Gas furnaces are the most common type in Canadian homes, so here is the gas furnace heating process from start to finish.

  1. The thermostat calls for heat. When the room temperature drops below your setting, the thermostat sends a low-voltage signal to the furnace control board.
  2. Safety checks begin. The control board starts the inducer motor, which clears the vent and creates draft. A pressure switch confirms the exhaust path is open before the process continues.
  3. The igniter warms up. The hot surface igniter or electronic ignition heats up so it is ready to light the gas.
  4. The gas valve opens and the burners light. Natural gas flows to the burners and ignites. The flame sensor confirms the flame is stable. If it does not detect a flame, the gas valve closes.
  5. The heat exchanger heats up. Hot combustion gases travel through the heat exchanger and warm its metal walls.
  6. The blower starts. After a short delay, once the heat exchanger is warm enough, the blower turns on. The delay prevents the system from blowing cold air into your rooms.
  7. Warm air travels through the ducts. The blower pushes air across the heat exchanger and sends it through the supply ducts to your vents, while the exhaust gases leave through the flue.
  8. The cycle ends. When the thermostat is satisfied, the gas valve closes and the burners shut off. The blower keeps running briefly to move the remaining heat out of the furnace, then stops.

High-efficiency condensing furnaces add a second heat exchanger that pulls extra heat out of the exhaust gases before they are vented. This is how many of these models reach efficiency ratings of 90% AFUE or higher, meaning most of the fuel becomes usable heat.

Understanding the Furnace Heating Cycle

The furnace heating cycle is one complete run of the steps above: from the thermostat calling for heat, through ignition and warm air delivery, to shutoff. On a cold day, your furnace may run several cycles an hour. On a mild day, it may run only a few short cycles.

Cycle length depends on the outdoor temperature, how well your home is insulated, the size of your furnace, and the type of system you have:

  • Single-stage furnaces run at full power every time, then shut off.
  • Two-stage furnaces can run on low for mild weather and switch to high when it gets colder.
  • Modulating furnaces adjust their output in small steps, which gives steadier temperatures and longer, quieter cycles.

What Is Short Cycling?

Short cycling happens when the furnace turns on and off again after only a few minutes, before the house has warmed up. It wears out parts faster and wastes energy. Common causes include a dirty furnace air filter, blocked vents, a poorly placed thermostat, an oversized furnace, or an overheating heat exchanger. If your furnace short cycles, replace the filter first. If the problem continues, book a service visit.

Keeping Your Furnace Working Well

A little care goes a long way. A well-maintained furnace typically lasts 15 to 20 years and runs more efficiently along the way.

  • Change the furnace air filter regularly. Check it monthly and replace it about every one to three months, or as your manufacturer recommends.
  • Book an annual tune-up. A technician can inspect the burners, heat exchanger, flame sensor, and venting before the cold season starts.
  • Keep vents and returns clear. Furniture and rugs over vents restrict airflow.
  • Test your thermostat. Replace its batteries if it uses them, and make sure it is set to heat.
  • Install carbon monoxide detectors. Place one on every level of your home and test them regularly.

Warning Signs to Watch For

  • Little or no warm air from the vents
  • Banging, rattling, or squealing noises
  • A yellow or flickering burner flame instead of a steady blue one
  • Frequent short cycling
  • A sudden jump in heating bills
  • A carbon monoxide alarm: leave the home immediately and call emergency services

If you notice any of these signs, contact a licensed heating professional rather than trying to repair gas components yourself.

Conclusion

So, how does a furnace work? The thermostat signals for heat, the burners ignite, the heat exchanger warms up, and the blower sends warm air through your ducts until the house reaches the temperature you set. Each of the furnace components has a job to do, and when they all work together, your home stays comfortable.

If your furnace is making odd noises, cycling too often, or is due for its yearly check, the team at Airlinx Heating is here to help. Contact us today to book a furnace inspection, repair, or replacement and keep your home warm all winter.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does a furnace work in simple terms?

A furnace burns fuel to heat a metal chamber called the heat exchanger. A blower pushes household air across that chamber, and the warmed air travels through your ducts to each room.

How long does a furnace heating cycle last?

It varies. Cold weather, a larger home, or poor insulation means longer cycles. Cycles that last only a minute or two are a sign of short cycling and are worth having checked.

Why does my furnace blower keep running?

The thermostat fan may be set to “On” instead of “Auto,” which runs the blower continuously. If it is set to Auto and the blower never stops, a faulty control or limit switch may be the cause, so call a technician.

How often should a furnace be serviced?

Once a year, ideally in the fall before the heating season begins.
